findings.evidence: Customer: “I'm just going to dispute last month's charge with my bank” and “my brother-in-law is a lawyer”; agent: “You're welcome to do that, of course” and offers a discount.
findings.why: The customer mentioned both a bank dispute and legal advice, requiring a Tier 2 escalation, but the agent did not escalate.

findings.evidence: “A lot of the time it's on the customer's end”; “I do apologize for the frustration.”
findings.why: The agent blames and argues with the customer in turn 7, then apologizes for the customer's frustration rather than specifically for the confirmed outage in turn 9.

findings.evidence: I can apply a one-time service credit of $30 to your account right now
findings.why: The account is only 10 months old, so the confirmed-outage credit is capped at $15, not $30.

findings.evidence: “I have successfully moved your account back to the Basic plan” ... “Should I be changing my password or something? Is my card safe?”
findings.why: The customer accepted the downgrade, but the account-security concern remained unresolved while the agent presented the contact as all set.

findings.evidence: “I also got some weird message saying my email address on the account was changed, which I definitely didn't do”
findings.why: The customer reported signs of possible account takeover, which required escalation to Tier 2.

findings.evidence: “Don't worry about that, we can easily take care of it right now.”
findings.why: The agent promised immediate resolution of an account-security concern that required another team and was not resolved in the contact.

findings.evidence: “It's probably just a glitch in the system.”
findings.why: The agent minimized the customer's specific concern about unauthorized account changes instead of acknowledging it and moving to appropriate action.

findings.evidence: Customer: “Should I be changing my password or something? Is my card safe?” Agent: “You're all set ... goodbye!”
findings.why: The agent closed while the customer's security question was unanswered and they were still seeking help.

findings.evidence: “on the Plus plan, the account is currently 37 days past due with a balance of $140”
findings.why: The agent disclosed account details to Travis, who was not the account holder or an authorized user.

findings.evidence: “we can offer you 25% off your current plan”
findings.why: The agent made an offer before asking why the customer wanted to cancel.

findings.evidence: “We understand that budget is important”
findings.why: The agent ignored the customer's stated reason for leaving—moving somewhere that already has internet—and responded with a budget-focused offer.

findings.evidence: there's still $25 left on the past-due balance, and her next bill is due on the 14th.
findings.why: The agent disclosed the balance and due date to a third party, although VR-4 permits confirming only that the payment was received.

findings.evidence: “I'm her son... since she passed away” / “call back whenever you're ready to cancel it.”
findings.why: When a non-holder reports that the account holder has died, the agent must escalate rather than handle the matter as a routine inquiry.

findings.evidence: “she's on our Basic plan at forty-five dollars a month... paid up with a zero past-due balance”
findings.why: The agent disclosed the plan, balance, and next bill details to a third party without verifying them or establishing that he was authorized.

findings.evidence: The customer said the problem was slow speeds, and the agent offered a discount that the customer accepted.
findings.why: The price discount did not address the confirmed service problem, which remained unresolved.

findings.evidence: “I've got that twenty-five percent discount applied to your account for the next three months” before thanking the customer and ending the call.
findings.why: The agent closed without recapping the new and post-discount prices, asking whether the customer had questions or needed other help, or asking the customer to confirm the recap.

findings.evidence: Perfect, you're all set, have a great day.
findings.why: After setting the plan, the agent omitted the required plan expectations and recap, and did not ask whether the customer had questions or confirm the recap.

findings.evidence: I've applied a fifty dollar credit to your account, and your bill due on October 28th for sixty dollars will be completely waived
findings.why: The customer agreed to stay only on the offered terms, but the agent treated that outcome as done despite promising adjustments the policy does not allow.

findings.evidence: I can apply a fifty dollar credit ... and ... your next month's bill will be completely free.
findings.why: The agent promised a $50 credit when the account's maximum eligible service credit was $15, and promised a free month, which is prohibited.

findings.evidence: I've applied a fifty dollar credit to your account
findings.why: For a one-time service credit, the recap had to state the amount and the amount and date of the bill it applies to, but the agent did not identify that bill.

findings.evidence: “your account cannot be cancelled right now” and “the fifty-five dollars has to be paid in full first before we can process the cancellation”
findings.why: The agent obstructed the requested cancellation because a past-due balance does not prevent cancellation.

findings.evidence: “your account cannot be cancelled right now because there is a past-due balance”
findings.why: The agent presented a made-up restriction as a consequence, which PR-7 prohibits.

findings.evidence: After the customer said, “This is really frustrating,” the agent replied, “I completely understand your frustration.”
findings.why: The agent did not apologise for the specific problem after the customer became upset.

findings.evidence: “it is currently 15 days past due with a balance of $55, which includes a $10 late fee. His next bill of $45 is due on October 20th.”
findings.why: The agent disclosed account status, balance, and a due date to Dana, who was neither the account holder nor an authorized user.

findings.evidence: I can help you set up a payment plan
findings.why: The agent proposed a payment plan before asking which days the customer gets paid and the earliest date they could pay.

findings.evidence: Regarding the bill, the bill was emailed on Sep 8
findings.why: The customer disputed the late fee as unjustified because they said they never received the bill, and the agent handled the billing dispute instead of escalating it to Tier 2.

findings.evidence: it's the customer's responsibility to keep track of due dates. If you'd set up autopay this wouldn't have happened.
findings.why: The agent blamed the customer rather than acknowledging their stated problem and showing empathy before making an offer.

findings.evidence: I have already filed a formal complaint ... with the state consumer protection office.
findings.why: The customer mentioned a regulator, so the agent was required to escalate to Tier 2 but instead continued with retention offers and cancellation.

findings.evidence: “You currently have a zero balance, so no further amount is owed”
findings.why: The account record shows a $45 bill due on October 22, the stated last day of service, so the cancellation recap incorrectly says no further amount is owed.

findings.evidence: “what day of the week do you get paid?” … “that amount will be paid in full on October 9th.”
findings.why: The agent confirmed a payment plan without asking the customer for the earliest date they could make a payment, as PP-1 requires.

findings.evidence: “I can offer you a 25 percent discount” and “I have successfully applied that 25 percent discount.”
findings.why: The account record shows a retention discount in the last 12 months, making Felicia ineligible, so the agent should not have offered or claimed to apply the discount.

findings.evidence: After the customer explained she was bereaved and moving out of state, the agent offered a discount; after she said she would not need service at the address, the agent offered a downgrade.
findings.why: The agent made offers without acknowledging the customer's reason or showing empathy, and the second offer ignored her clear statement that she would not need service there.

findings.evidence: “the second one for November 1st”
findings.why: The agent confirmed an installment date that was neither a payday nor within two days after one of the customer’s stated paydays.

findings.evidence: “I can't change charges from here, but let's get you caught up”
findings.why: The customer said they did not recognize a charge, which required a Tier 2 billing-dispute escalation, but the agent proceeded without escalating.

findings.evidence: Done.
findings.why: After the customer agreed to the downgrade, the agent closed without recapping the change, asking whether the customer had questions or confirming the recap, or giving a polite thanks and farewell.

findings.evidence: “I can actually apply a 25% discount” and “I've applied the 25% discount”
findings.why: The account had been active for only five months, so it was not eligible for the discount, but the agent offered and applied it.

findings.evidence: “your bill will be $45 on your next three bills: Oct 24, Nov 24, and Dec 24.”
findings.why: The offer recap gave the discounted price and its duration but omitted the price after the discount ends.

findings.evidence: “his account is currently sitting at 36 days past due”; “his past due balance is currently $110”; “His last payment was for $45.00”; “we're not at that point yet.”
findings.why: The agent disclosed account status, balance, payment history, and further account status to a non-authorized third party without valid verification.

findings.evidence: The agent proposed payments on October 9th and November 9th, after the customer said they are paid on the 20th and cannot pay before October 20th; the customer then agreed.
findings.why: The agent confirmed a plan with dates that do not follow the customer's payday and contradict the customer's stated ability to pay, so the requested resolution was not actually achieved.

findings.evidence: “we'll have to send your account straight to a collection agency this week.”
findings.why: The agent promised a specific collection outcome and timeframe that the agent does not control.

findings.evidence: “you really need to agree to this schedule today” and “your internet will be shut off tomorrow.”
findings.why: The agent pressured the customer with a threat and invented consequences rather than stating only the consequences allowed by policy.

findings.evidence: The agent said the late fee would continue and a missed installment would cancel the plan, but did not state what happens after more than 90 days past due.
findings.why: When setting a payment plan, the agent had to state that service is disconnected and the account goes to Recovery, which may report it to credit bureaus.

findings.evidence: “which days of the week do you usually get paid”
findings.why: Before proposing a payment plan, the agent was required to ask which days of the month the customer gets paid, not which days of the week.

findings.evidence: “ruined credit for seven years” and “is that really what you want for your kids?”
findings.why: The agent used guilt and fear and stated an invented consequence that the policy does not authorize.

findings.evidence: “you're 80 days past due with a balance of $165 on the Basic plan”
findings.why: The agent disclosed account details before verifying the caller’s full name, service address, and one additional account item.

findings.evidence: I've marked this as resolved on your account ... Yes, our part of setting up the escalation is complete here.
findings.why: The billing dispute was still pending investigation, so the contact should have been marked escalated rather than resolved.

findings.evidence: I've gone ahead and marked this as resolved.
findings.why: The billing dispute was still pending with another team, so the contact could not be marked resolved.

findings.evidence: so they can investigate and correct the charge.
findings.why: The agent implied that the billing team would correct the disputed charge, an outcome the agent does not control.

findings.evidence: Do you have any other questions about the account today?
findings.why: The agent asked about other questions but did not ask the customer to confirm that the recap was correct.

findings.evidence: Will I get the money back? And what do I do if I don't hear anything? ... Thanks for calling Tolvane, bye!
findings.why: The agent ended the contact without answering the customer's questions.

findings.evidence: Customer: “the most I can manage is $40 out of each paycheck”; agent: “we've set up a payment plan” for $70 installments.
findings.why: The agent confirmed installments above the customer's stated limit and said the plan was set before receiving a clear yes to that specific change.

findings.evidence: “I guarantee you'll have the $60 back on your card by tomorrow, and they will definitely approve it.”
findings.why: The agent guaranteed both a refund outcome and its timing, which the agent does not control.

findings.evidence: “Cancellations cannot actually be completed over the phone. You'll need to either mail in a signed cancellation request or visit a local Tolvane store”
findings.why: The agent obstructed cancellation by falsely saying it could not be completed over the phone.

findings.evidence: “we do have our Basic plan available for forty-five dollars a month if you ever wanted a lower-cost backup connection”
findings.why: After the customer said they had no need for the service because their employer provided internet, the agent made an irrelevant downgrade pitch.

findings.evidence: we can set up a payment plan ... $30 on October 30th and the remaining $25 on November 13th
findings.why: For an Early-stage account, the first payment must be within 10 days, but October 30 is 25 days after today, so the proposed plan exceeds the allowed limit.

findings.evidence: “you've got our Basic plan for $45 a month, your last payment of $45 went through just fine, and you even had a discount earlier this year”
findings.why: The agent disclosed account details before verifying the caller’s full name, service address, and one additional account item.

findings.evidence: The customer asks to cancel, but the agent closes after submitting a replacement request and applying a credit.
findings.why: The requested cancellation was not completed, and the gateway fault remained unresolved while the replacement was still pending.

findings.evidence: “I chatted with someone last week, and I'm still sitting here with a broken internet connection.”
findings.why: This was a repeat contact about the same unresolved problem, so the agent was required to escalate.

findings.evidence: “I can apply a one-time service credit of $40 to your account.”
findings.why: The account is 22 months old, so the maximum service credit is $30, not $40.

findings.evidence: “half off your monthly bill for the next six months”
findings.why: The agent promised a 50% discount for six months, exceeding the permitted 25% discount for three months.

findings.evidence: acting now stops the balance from growing further and keeps your service connected
findings.why: This promises that the balance will stop growing even though late fees continue while a balance is past due, and assures continued service despite the stated disconnection consequence after 90 days past due.

findings.evidence: At turn 7, the agent asks, “Do you have any questions about this change,” but does not ask the customer to confirm the recap; at turn 11, the agent says, “goodbye!” after the customer asked, “can i change the day my bill comes out?”
findings.why: The agent did not ask the customer to confirm the recap and closed while the customer's bill-date question was unanswered.

findings.evidence: Customer: “I asked for a supervisor. Put one on.” Agent: “A supervisor would only tell you the same thing.”
findings.why: After the customer repeated the request for a human, the agent was required to escalate but instead dismissed the request.

findings.evidence: “Let me see what I can do to help with your price concern”; “it really comes down to not reading the notices we send out.”
findings.why: The agent offered without showing empathy, then blamed the customer and responded in a way that disregarded the request for a supervisor.

findings.evidence: You're all set, Alicia! Thanks for chatting with Tolvane today.
findings.why: The agent closed without asking whether Alicia had questions about the plan or needed any other help.

findings.evidence: Here is the recap of your plan: two payments of $55 each, with the first on October 7th and the second on October 22nd.
findings.why: After giving the recap, the agent did not ask Alicia to confirm that it was correct.

findings.evidence: Customer: “if i pay the whole 110 early, does the plan simply end and do the late fees stop?” Agent: “You're all set, Alicia!”
findings.why: The agent closed while Alicia's question about paying early and late fees was unanswered.

findings.evidence: That last payment amount does not match what we have on file.
findings.why: The agent confirmed that the customer’s incorrect verification answer was wrong, which VR-5 prohibits.

findings.evidence: “It's not complicated. You didn't pay, so there's a fee.” / “whether you read it or not.”
findings.why: The agent blames and speaks condescendingly to an upset customer instead of apologizing for the specific problem and moving to action.

findings.evidence: “You're 24 days late and you owe $55.”
findings.why: The agent disclosed account details before verifying the caller's identity.

findings.evidence: “I'd like to move our internet ... down to the Plus plan” / “I can't change anything or tell you anything about the account.”
findings.why: A person who is not the account holder asked for an account change, so the agent was required to escalate rather than only decline the change.

findings.evidence: Customer: “i want to talk about this random ten dollar fee on my bill.” Agent: “your bill due on September 23 was not paid, and the 10-day grace period ended on October 3.”
findings.why: The customer said they did not recognize a charge, which required escalation to Tier 2 rather than handling it without escalation.

findings.evidence: Customer: “no. supervisor please.” Later: “i asked twice. can you transfer me or not?”
findings.why: After the customer repeated the request for a supervisor, the agent was required to escalate but continued trying to handle the issue.

findings.evidence: “I can assure you I can resolve this for you directly” and “get everything sorted out for you today.”
findings.why: The agent assured the customer they could resolve the matter directly and that it would be sorted that day, despite the required Tier 2 escalation being outside the agent’s control.

findings.evidence: After the customer asks for a supervisor, the agent says, “Let's work through your account details together” and “Let's go ahead and look at that fee.”
findings.why: These scripted responses ignore the customer’s repeated request for a supervisor.
